femur.summary: The thigh bone: the longest and strongest bone in the body, running from the hip joint to the knee.
femur.function: Carries the weight of the trunk to the leg and anchors the muscles of the hip and thigh; its head sits in the acetabulum of the hip bone and its condyles form the knee with the tibia.
femur.clinical: Hip fractures through the femoral neck are common in older adults with osteoporosis; the femoral shaft breaks only with major force.

tibia.summary: The shin bone: the larger, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg, from the knee to the ankle.
tibia.function: Transmits body weight from the femur to the talus; its sharp anterior border lies just under the skin of the shin.
tibia.clinical: Tibial shaft fractures are the commonest long-bone fractures; stress fractures affect runners.

fibula.summary: The slender lateral bone of the lower leg, running beside the tibia to form the outer ankle (lateral malleolus).
fibula.function: Bears little weight but anchors leg muscles and stabilises the ankle joint.
fibula.clinical: The lateral malleolus is broken in many ankle fractures; the fibula is also harvested for bone grafts.

patella.summary: The kneecap: a triangular sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee.
patella.function: Increases the leverage of the quadriceps and protects the front of the knee joint.
patella.clinical: Patellar dislocation and patellofemoral pain are common in young, active people.

hip bone.summary: The large, irregular bone formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis; the two hip bones and the sacrum make up the bony pelvis.
hip bone.function: Transfers the weight of the upper body to the legs through the hip joint (acetabulum) and protects the pelvic organs.
hip bone.clinical: Pelvic fractures usually follow high-energy trauma; the iliac crest is a common site for bone-marrow sampling.

sacrum.summary: A triangular bone formed by five fused sacral vertebrae, wedged between the hip bones at the base of the spine.
sacrum.function: Transmits the weight of the trunk to the pelvis and completes the posterior wall of the pelvis.
sacrum.clinical: The sacroiliac joints are a frequent source of low back pain.

humerus.summary: The bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
humerus.function: Its rounded head articulates with the scapula's glenoid cavity; the distal end forms the elbow with the radius and ulna. It anchors the deltoid, biceps and triceps.
humerus.clinical: Fractures of the surgical neck (in older adults) and shaft may injure the axillary or radial nerve.

radius.summary: The lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side, wider at the wrist than at the elbow.
radius.function: Rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down (supination and pronation) and carries most of the load across the wrist joint.
radius.clinical: A fall on the outstretched hand often breaks the distal radius (Colles fracture).

ulna.summary: The medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side, with the olecranon forming the point of the elbow.
ulna.function: Forms the hinge of the elbow with the humerus and the pivot around which the radius rotates.
ulna.clinical: The olecranon can be fractured by a direct blow to the elbow.

clavicle.summary: The collarbone: an S-shaped bone running from the sternum to the acromion of the scapula.
clavicle.function: Acts as a strut holding the shoulder away from the chest so the arm can swing freely; it is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
clavicle.clinical: One of the most frequently fractured bones, usually in its middle third after a fall on the shoulder.

scapula.summary: The shoulder blade: a flat triangular bone lying against the back of the rib cage.
scapula.function: Its glenoid cavity forms the shoulder joint with the humerus; its spine and acromion anchor the deltoid and trapezius, and it glides over the ribs to widen the reach of the arm.
scapula.clinical: Scapular fractures are rare and signal severe chest trauma.

body of sternum.summary: The long middle part of the breastbone, lying in the front of the chest.
body of sternum.function: Anchors the costal cartilages of ribs 2 to 7 and protects the heart behind it.
body of sternum.clinical: The sternum is split lengthways for open-heart surgery and is a site for bone-marrow sampling.

manubrium.summary: The upper, wider part of the sternum, joined to the clavicles and the first ribs.
manubrium.function: Forms the sternoclavicular joints; the notch at its top can be felt at the base of the neck.
manubrium.clinical: The junction with the body of the sternum (sternal angle) is a landmark for counting ribs.

xiphoid process.summary: The small, pointed lower tip of the sternum, cartilaginous in youth and bony in later life.
xiphoid process.function: Gives attachment to the diaphragm, the linea alba and the rectus abdominis.
xiphoid process.clinical: Hand position for CPR is judged from the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid.

atlas.summary: C1, the first cervical vertebra: a ring of bone without a body that supports the skull.
atlas.function: Its joints with the occipital condyles allow nodding; the axis's dens pivots inside it for head rotation.
atlas.clinical: A Jefferson fracture is a burst of the atlas ring after an axial load to the head.

axis.summary: C2, the second cervical vertebra, with a tooth-like dens projecting upward into the atlas.
axis.function: The dens forms the pivot that lets the head turn from side to side.
axis.clinical: Fractures of the dens are common neck injuries in falls, especially in the elderly.

frontal bone.summary: The bone of the forehead and the roof of the orbits.
frontal bone.function: Protects the frontal lobes and forms the upper margins of the eye sockets; it contains the frontal sinuses.
frontal bone.clinical: Frontal sinusitis and forehead fractures may involve the underlying brain.

parietal bone.summary: One of a pair of large curved bones forming the sides and roof of the skull.
parietal bone.function: Protects the parietal lobes of the brain.
parietal bone.clinical: Skull fractures here can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an extradural haematoma.

temporal bone.summary: A complex bone at the side and base of the skull housing the ear.
temporal bone.function: Contains the middle and inner ear, forms the jaw joint with the mandible and gives attachment to neck muscles through the mastoid process.
temporal bone.clinical: Temporal bone fractures may cause hearing loss or facial nerve palsy.

occipital bone.summary: The bone at the back and base of the skull, pierced by the foramen magnum.
occipital bone.function: Protects the occipital lobes and cerebellum; the spinal cord passes through the foramen magnum, and the occipital condyles rest on the atlas.
occipital bone.clinical: Fractures of the skull base can leak cerebrospinal fluid from the ear or nose.

ethmoid.summary: A light, spongy bone between the orbits forming the roof of the nasal cavity.
ethmoid.function: Its cribriform plate is pierced by the olfactory nerves; its air cells form the ethmoidal sinuses.
ethmoid.clinical: Fractures of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell and cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

maxilla.summary: The upper jaw bone, holding the upper teeth and forming much of the face.
maxilla.function: Forms the floor of the orbit, the side of the nose and the hard palate; contains the maxillary sinus.
maxilla.clinical: Maxillary sinusitis is the commonest sinus infection; Le Fort fractures separate the maxilla from the skull.

mandible.summary: The lower jaw, the largest and strongest bone of the face and the only movable skull bone.
mandible.function: Holds the lower teeth and articulates with the temporal bones at the jaw joints; the muscles of mastication move it.
mandible.clinical: Mandibular fractures are common in assaults; the temporomandibular joint is a frequent source of facial pain.

zygomatic bone.summary: The cheekbone, forming the prominence of the cheek and the outer wall of the orbit.
zygomatic bone.function: Protects the eye and gives origin to the masseter muscle.
zygomatic bone.clinical: Zygomatic fractures flatten the cheek and may trap eye muscles.

nasal bone.summary: One of two small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
nasal bone.function: Supports the upper part of the nose.
nasal bone.clinical: The most frequently fractured facial bone.

lacrimal bone.summary: The smallest bone of the face, in the inner wall of the orbit.
lacrimal bone.function: Houses the lacrimal sac, which drains tears into the nose.

palatine bone.summary: An L-shaped bone forming the back of the hard palate and part of the nasal cavity and orbit.
palatine bone.function: Separates the mouth from the nasal cavity.

vomer.summary: A thin, plough-shaped bone forming the lower back part of the nasal septum.
vomer.function: Divides the nasal cavity into left and right halves.
vomer.clinical: A deviated septum can block airflow through one nostril.

inferior nasal concha.summary: A scroll-shaped bone projecting into the nasal cavity from its lateral wall.
inferior nasal concha.function: Increases the surface area that warms and humidifies inhaled air.

hyoid bone.summary: A U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, unique in articulating with no other bone.
hyoid bone.function: Suspended by muscles and ligaments, it anchors the tongue and larynx during swallowing and speech.
hyoid bone.clinical: A fractured hyoid is a classic sign of strangulation.

scaphoid.summary: The boat-shaped carpal bone on the thumb side of the wrist.
scaphoid.function: Links the two rows of carpal bones and bears load across the wrist.
scaphoid.clinical: The most commonly fractured carpal bone; its poor blood supply makes non-union and avascular necrosis a risk.

lunate.summary: The crescent-shaped carpal bone in the centre of the proximal row.
lunate.function: Articulates with the radius to form the main part of the wrist joint.
lunate.clinical: Lunate dislocation and Kienbock's disease (avascular necrosis) affect this bone.

pisiform.summary: A pea-sized sesamoid bone in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
pisiform.function: Increases the leverage of flexor carpi ulnaris and forms a wall of the ulnar canal.

trapezium.summary: The carpal bone at the base of the thumb.
trapezium.function: Its saddle-shaped joint with the first metacarpal gives the thumb its wide range of movement.
trapezium.clinical: Osteoarthritis of the trapeziometacarpal joint causes pain at the base of the thumb.

trapezoid.summary: A small wedge-shaped carpal bone at the base of the index finger.

capitate.summary: The largest carpal bone, in the centre of the wrist.
capitate.function: Articulates with the third metacarpal and forms the keystone of the carpal arch.

hamate.summary: The wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side with a hook projecting into the palm.
hamate.function: The hook forms part of the carpal tunnel and anchors the flexor retinaculum.
hamate.clinical: Hook of hamate fractures occur in golfers and racquet sports.

talus.summary: The ankle bone, sitting on the calcaneus and gripped between the tibia and fibula.
talus.function: Transmits the whole weight of the body from the leg to the foot; it has no muscle attachments.
talus.clinical: Talar fractures risk avascular necrosis because of the bone's limited blood supply.

calcaneus.summary: The heel bone, the largest bone of the foot.
calcaneus.function: Forms the heel, bears weight on standing and anchors the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
calcaneus.clinical: Fractured in falls from height; plantar fasciitis causes pain at its underside.

cuboid bone.summary: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the outer side of the midfoot.
cuboid bone.function: Supports the lateral arch and provides a groove for the tendon of fibularis longus.

skin.summary: The outer covering of the body and its largest organ, shown here as a translucent shell.
skin.function: Barrier against infection and water loss, the organ of touch and temperature sensation, and a regulator of body heat.
skin.clinical: Wounds, burns, infections and skin cancers all begin at this surface.

hair of head.summary: The scalp hair, modelled as a single surface.
hair of head.function: Insulates the scalp and protects it from sunlight.

eyebrow.summary: The arch of hair above each eye.
eyebrow.function: Diverts sweat and rain away from the eye and plays a large role in facial expression.

pubic hair.summary: Hair of the pubic region, a secondary sexual characteristic that appears at puberty in every sex under the influence of androgens.

deltoid.summary: The thick triangular muscle capping the shoulder, with clavicular, acromial and spinal parts.
deltoid.function: Its middle fibres abduct the arm; the front and back fibres flex and extend it.
deltoid.clinical: Common site for intramuscular injections; wasting follows axillary nerve injury.

pectoralis major.summary: The large fan-shaped muscle of the chest, with clavicular, sternocostal and abdominal parts.
pectoralis major.function: Adducts and medially rotates the arm and helps flex it; used in pushing and climbing.

pectoralis minor.summary: A thin triangular muscle beneath pectoralis major, from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process.
pectoralis minor.function: Pulls the scapula forward and down and helps lift the ribs in forced breathing.

biceps brachii.summary: The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm, from the scapula to the radius.
biceps brachii.function: Flexes the elbow and, most powerfully, supinates the forearm (turning the palm up).
biceps brachii.clinical: Rupture of the long head tendon produces a 'Popeye' bulge in the arm.

triceps brachii.summary: The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm, inserting on the olecranon of the ulna.
triceps brachii.function: The main extensor of the elbow, essential for pushing and throwing.
triceps brachii.clinical: Supplied by the radial nerve; weakness of extension follows radial nerve injury.

brachialis.summary: A broad muscle lying under the biceps, from the humerus to the ulna.
brachialis.function: The strongest flexor of the elbow, working in every position of the forearm.

brachioradialis.summary: The muscle forming the bulk of the lateral forearm, from the humerus to the distal radius.
brachioradialis.function: Flexes the elbow, most effectively with the forearm midway between pronation and supination.

coracobrachialis.summary: A small muscle from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus.
coracobrachialis.function: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.

anconeus.summary: A small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow.
anconeus.function: Assists triceps in extending the elbow and stabilises the joint.

supraspinatus.summary: A rotator cuff muscle running above the spine of the scapula to the top of the humerus.
supraspinatus.function: Starts abduction of the arm and holds the humeral head in the glenoid.
supraspinatus.clinical: The most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon; impingement under the acromion causes painful arc.

infraspinatus muscle.summary: A rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the scapula.
infraspinatus muscle.function: Laterally rotates the arm and stabilises the shoulder.

teres minor.summary: A small rotator cuff muscle along the lateral border of the scapula.
teres minor.function: Laterally rotates the arm with infraspinatus.

teres major.summary: A thick muscle from the lower scapula to the front of the humerus.
teres major.function: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm, working with latissimus dorsi.

subscapularis.summary: The rotator cuff muscle filling the front surface of the scapula.
subscapularis.function: Medially rotates the arm and prevents the humeral head sliding forward.

trapezius.summary: The large kite-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck, with descending, transverse and ascending parts.
trapezius.function: Elevates, retracts and depresses the scapula and rotates it to raise the arm overhead.
trapezius.clinical: Its upper fibres carry much of the tension of neck and shoulder pain.

rhomboid major.summary: A flat muscle between the thoracic spine and the medial border of the scapula.
rhomboid major.function: Retracts the scapula, squaring the shoulders.

rhomboid minor.summary: A small muscle above rhomboid major, from C7 and T1 to the scapula.

levator scapulae.summary: A strap muscle from the upper cervical vertebrae to the top corner of the scapula.
levator scapulae.function: Elevates the scapula, as in shrugging.
levator scapulae.clinical: A common site of tension in neck pain.

serratus anterior.summary: A muscle wrapping around the side of the chest from the upper ribs to the scapula.
serratus anterior.function: Pulls the scapula forward and rotates it upward, essential for punching and lifting the arm above the head.
serratus anterior.clinical: Long thoracic nerve injury causes a 'winged' scapula.

subclavius.summary: A small muscle under the clavicle, from the first rib.
subclavius.function: Steadies the clavicle during shoulder movements.

sternocleidomastoid.summary: The prominent strap muscle on each side of the neck, from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process.
sternocleidomastoid.function: Turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it to the same side; both together flex the neck.
sternocleidomastoid.clinical: Torticollis (wry neck) results from spasm or shortening of this muscle.

scalenus anterior.summary: A neck muscle from the cervical vertebrae to the first rib.
scalenus anterior.function: Lifts the first rib in breathing and bends the neck sideways.
scalenus anterior.clinical: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes; tightness can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.

scalenus medius.summary: The largest of the scalene muscles, from the cervical vertebrae to the first rib.
scalenus medius.function: Elevates the first rib and flexes the neck laterally.

scalenus posterior.summary: The smallest scalene muscle, reaching the second rib.
scalenus posterior.function: Elevates the second rib and bends the neck sideways.

platysma.summary: A broad, thin sheet of muscle in the superficial tissue of the neck.
platysma.function: Tenses the skin of the neck and draws down the corners of the mouth.

diaphragm.summary: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle separating the chest from the abdomen.
diaphragm.function: The main muscle of breathing: contracting flattens the dome, enlarging the chest and drawing air in. Openings carry the aorta, oesophagus and inferior vena cava.
diaphragm.clinical: Hiatus hernia lets the stomach slide through the oesophageal opening; the phrenic nerves that drive it arise from C3 to C5.

external intercostal muscle.summary: The outermost layer of muscle between the ribs, with fibres running downward and forward.

internal intercostal muscle.summary: The middle layer of muscle between the ribs, with fibres running downward and backward.
internal intercostal muscle.function: Pulls the ribs down in forced expiration.

innermost intercostal muscle.summary: The deepest layer between the ribs, separated from the internal intercostals by the intercostal nerves and vessels.
innermost intercostal muscle.function: Assists the internal intercostals in expiration.

transversus thoracis.summary: A thin muscle on the inside of the front of the rib cage.
transversus thoracis.function: Draws the costal cartilages down in expiration.

external oblique.summary: The largest and most superficial of the flat abdominal muscles, with fibres running like hands in pockets.
external oblique.function: Compresses the abdomen, flexes and rotates the trunk, and helps forced expiration.
external oblique.clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the outer ring of the inguinal canal.

linea alba.summary: The tendinous seam running down the midline of the abdomen from the xiphoid to the pubis.
linea alba.function: Joins the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal muscles of both sides.
linea alba.clinical: Midline surgical incisions pass through it; it may widen after pregnancy (diastasis).

psoas major.summary: A long muscle from the lumbar spine that joins the iliacus to insert on the femur.
psoas major.function: The most powerful flexor of the hip; also flexes the lumbar spine.
psoas major.clinical: A psoas abscess can track down from the spine; hip flexor tightness is common in sedentary people.

iliacus.summary: A fan-shaped muscle filling the inside of the ilium.
iliacus.function: Joins psoas major (as iliopsoas) to flex the hip.

gluteus maximus.summary: The largest and most superficial muscle of the buttock.
gluteus maximus.function: The main extensor of the hip, used in climbing stairs, rising from a chair and running.
gluteus maximus.clinical: Site of intramuscular injections in the upper outer quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve.

gluteus medius.summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the outer side of the hip, partly under gluteus maximus.
gluteus medius.function: Abducts the hip and keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
gluteus medius.clinical: Weakness produces a Trendelenburg gait, with the pelvis dropping on the opposite side.

gluteus minimus.summary: The smallest and deepest of the gluteal muscles.
gluteus minimus.function: Abducts and medially rotates the hip and steadies the pelvis in walking.

tensor fasciae latae.summary: A short muscle at the front of the hip inserting into the iliotibial tract.
tensor fasciae latae.function: Tenses the iliotibial tract, helping to abduct and flex the hip and steady the knee.

iliotibial tract.summary: A thick band of fascia running down the outer thigh from the hip to the tibia.
iliotibial tract.function: Stabilises the knee in standing and walking.
iliotibial tract.clinical: Iliotibial band syndrome causes lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists.

piriformis.summary: A pear-shaped muscle from the sacrum to the greater trochanter, leaving the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
piriformis.function: Laterally rotates and abducts the hip.
piriformis.clinical: The sciatic nerve passes beneath (occasionally through) it; piriformis syndrome mimics sciatica.

obturator internus.summary: A muscle lining the inside of the pelvis that turns sharply to reach the femur.
obturator internus.function: Laterally rotates the hip and steadies the femoral head.

obturator externus.summary: A flat muscle on the outer surface of the obturator membrane.

gemellus superior.summary: A small muscle running with the obturator internus tendon.

gemellus inferior.summary: A small muscle below the obturator internus tendon.

quadratus femoris.summary: A flat, square muscle from the ischium to the femur.

rectus femoris.summary: The straight head of the quadriceps, running down the front of the thigh from the hip bone to the patella.
rectus femoris.function: Extends the knee and, uniquely among the quadriceps, also flexes the hip; used in kicking.
rectus femoris.clinical: Prone to strains in sprinters and footballers.

vastus lateralis.summary: The largest part of the quadriceps, on the outer thigh.
vastus lateralis.clinical: Preferred site for intramuscular injections in infants.

vastus medialis.summary: The part of the quadriceps on the inner thigh, bulging just above the knee.
vastus medialis.function: Extends the knee and steadies the patella in its groove.
vastus medialis.clinical: Wastes quickly after knee injury; strengthening it helps patellar tracking.

vastus intermedius.summary: The deep part of the quadriceps, lying on the front of the femur under rectus femoris.

sartorius.summary: The longest muscle in the body, winding from the front of the hip bone across the thigh to the inner knee.
sartorius.function: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee, the movement of crossing the legs.

gracilis.summary: A long, thin muscle on the inner thigh from the pubis to the tibia.
gracilis.function: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
gracilis.clinical: Often harvested for tendon and muscle grafts.

pectineus.summary: A flat muscle at the top of the inner thigh, from the pubis to the femur.

adductor longus.summary: The most superficial adductor, from the pubis to the middle of the femur.
adductor longus.function: Adducts the thigh, bringing the legs together.
adductor longus.clinical: The usual site of 'groin strain' in football and hockey.

adductor brevis.summary: A short adductor muscle beneath adductor longus.
adductor brevis.function: Adducts the thigh and assists hip flexion.

adductor magnus.summary: The largest adductor, a broad triangular sheet on the inner thigh with an adductor and a hamstring part.
adductor magnus.function: Adducts the thigh; its hamstring part extends the hip.
adductor magnus.clinical: The femoral artery passes through its adductor hiatus to reach the back of the knee.

adductor minimus.summary: The upper, partly separate portion of adductor magnus.
adductor minimus.function: Adducts and laterally rotates the thigh.

biceps femoris.summary: The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischium and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibula.
biceps femoris.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip; the main lateral rotator of the flexed knee.
biceps femoris.clinical: Hamstring tears are the commonest sprinting injury.

semitendinosus.summary: A medial hamstring with a long cord-like tendon reaching the tibia.
semitendinosus.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip.
semitendinosus.clinical: Its tendon is commonly used to reconstruct the anterior cruciate ligament.

semimembranosus.summary: The deepest medial hamstring, with a broad flat tendon of origin.
semimembranosus.function: Flexes the knee, extends the hip and medially rotates the flexed leg.

gastrocnemius.summary: The two-headed calf muscle forming the bulge of the calf, from the femoral condyles to the Achilles tendon.
gastrocnemius.function: Plantar flexes the ankle (rising on the toes) and helps flex the knee; the power muscle of walking, running and jumping.
gastrocnemius.clinical: 'Tennis leg' is a tear of the medial head; calf strains are common in sport.

soleus.summary: A broad flat muscle beneath gastrocnemius, from the tibia and fibula.
soleus.function: Plantar flexes the ankle and keeps the body from toppling forward when standing; its pumping action returns venous blood from the leg.

plantaris.summary: A small muscle with a very long thin tendon running beside the Achilles tendon.
plantaris.function: A weak plantar flexor; its tendon is sometimes used as a graft.

calcaneal tendon.summary: The Achilles tendon: the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, from the calf muscles to the heel.
calcaneal tendon.function: Transmits the pull of gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus to lift the heel.
calcaneal tendon.clinical: Rupture feels like a kick to the back of the ankle; tendinopathy affects runners.

popliteus.summary: A small muscle at the back of the knee.
popliteus.function: 'Unlocks' the extended knee by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia at the start of flexion.

tibialis anterior.summary: The muscle beside the shin bone on the front of the leg.
tibialis anterior.function: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot, lifting the toes in walking.
tibialis anterior.clinical: Weakness (foot drop) follows common fibular nerve injury; shin splints affect its attachment.

tibialis posterior.summary: The deepest muscle of the calf, its tendon passing behind the inner ankle.
tibialis posterior.function: Inverts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the medial arch.
tibialis posterior.clinical: Tendon failure leads to a progressive flat foot in adults.

extensor digitorum longus.summary: A muscle on the front of the leg whose tendons reach the four lesser toes.
extensor digitorum longus.function: Extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.

extensor hallucis longus.summary: A deep muscle of the front of the leg with a tendon to the big toe.
extensor hallucis longus.function: Extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the ankle.
extensor hallucis longus.clinical: Its strength tests the L5 nerve root.

extensor hallucis brevis.summary: A small muscle on the top of the foot reaching the big toe.

flexor digitorum longus.summary: A deep calf muscle whose tendons cross the sole to the four lesser toes.
flexor digitorum longus.function: Flexes the toes and helps plantar flex the foot.

flexor hallucis longus.summary: A deep calf muscle from the fibula with a tendon to the big toe.
flexor hallucis longus.function: Flexes the big toe, giving the final push-off in walking.

flexor hallucis brevis.summary: A short muscle in the sole with two heads inserting on the big toe.
flexor hallucis brevis.function: Flexes the big toe at its base.

fibularis longus.summary: A muscle on the outer side of the leg whose tendon crosses under the sole to the first metatarsal.
fibularis longus.function: Everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arches.
fibularis longus.clinical: Its nerve, the superficial fibular nerve, is injured by ankle sprains.

fibularis brevis.summary: A muscle of the outer leg inserting on the base of the fifth metatarsal.
fibularis brevis.function: Everts the foot and steadies the ankle.
fibularis brevis.clinical: Violent inversion can avulse the fifth metatarsal base at its attachment.

fibularis tertius.summary: A small muscle beside extensor digitorum longus reaching the fifth metatarsal.

abductor hallucis.summary: A muscle along the inner border of the sole.
abductor hallucis.function: Abducts and flexes the big toe and supports the medial arch.

flexor accessorius.summary: Quadratus plantae: a muscle of the sole attached to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
flexor accessorius.function: Straightens the pull of flexor digitorum longus on the toes.

flexor digitorum brevis.summary: A muscle in the middle of the sole with tendons to the four lesser toes.
flexor digitorum brevis.function: Flexes the toes at their middle joints.

abductor digiti minimi of foot.summary: A muscle along the outer border of the sole.
abductor digiti minimi of foot.function: Abducts and flexes the little toe.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot.summary: A small muscle of the sole reaching the little toe.

opponens digiti minimi of foot.summary: A small, often incomplete muscle of the sole beside the fifth metatarsal.
opponens digiti minimi of foot.function: Draws the fifth metatarsal toward the sole.

adductor hallucis.summary: A muscle of the sole with an oblique and a transverse head inserting on the big toe.
adductor hallucis.function: Adducts the big toe and supports the transverse arch.

pronator teres.summary: A muscle crossing the front of the forearm from the medial epicondyle and ulna to the radius.
pronator teres.function: Pronates the forearm (turns the palm down) and helps flex the elbow.
pronator teres.clinical: The median nerve passes between its two heads.

pronator quadratus.summary: A square muscle across the front of the distal forearm.
pronator quadratus.function: The main pronator of the forearm.

supinator.summary: A muscle wrapping around the upper radius.
supinator.function: Supinates the forearm, especially when the elbow is straight.
supinator.clinical: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes through it.

flexor carpi radialis.summary: A forearm muscle from the medial epicondyle to the base of the second and third metacarpals.
flexor carpi radialis.clinical: The radial pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon.

flexor carpi ulnaris.summary: The most medial forearm flexor, inserting on the pisiform.
flexor carpi ulnaris.clinical: The ulnar nerve runs beneath it in the forearm.

palmaris longus.summary: A slender forearm muscle inserting into the palmar aponeurosis, absent in about one person in seven.
palmaris longus.function: Weakly flexes the wrist and tenses the palm.
palmaris longus.clinical: Its tendon is a favourite graft for hand surgery.

flexor digitorum superficialis.summary: A large forearm muscle whose four tendons split to insert on the middle phalanges.
flexor digitorum superficialis.function: Flexes the middle joints of the fingers and the wrist.

flexor digitorum profundus.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendons pass through those of the superficialis to reach the fingertips.
flexor digitorum profundus.function: Flexes the fingertips; the only muscle that can flex the distal joints.

flexor pollicis longus.summary: A deep forearm muscle from the radius to the tip of the thumb.
flexor pollicis longus.function: Flexes the thumb tip, as in pinching.

extensor carpi radialis longus.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the second metacarpal.
extensor carpi radialis longus.function: Extends and abducts the wrist, as in making a fist.

extensor carpi radialis brevis.summary: A muscle on the back of the forearm to the third metacarpal.
extensor carpi radialis brevis.clinical: Its origin at the lateral epicondyle is the site of tennis elbow.

extensor carpi ulnaris.summary: A muscle along the ulnar side of the back of the forearm to the fifth metacarpal.

extensor digitorum.summary: The main extensor of the fingers, whose tendons fan across the back of the hand.

extensor digiti minimi.summary: A slender muscle with a tendon to the little finger.

extensor indicis.summary: A deep forearm muscle with a tendon to the index finger.
extensor indicis.function: Extends the index finger independently, as in pointing.

extensor pollicis longus.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
extensor pollicis longus.function: Extends the thumb tip and lifts the thumb away from the palm.

extensor pollicis brevis.summary: A small muscle with a tendon to the base of the thumb.
extensor pollicis brevis.function: Extends the thumb at its middle joint.
extensor pollicis brevis.clinical: Inflamed with abductor pollicis longus in De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

abductor pollicis longus.summary: A deep forearm muscle whose tendon reaches the first metacarpal.
abductor pollicis longus.function: Abducts and extends the thumb at its base.

abductor pollicis brevis.summary: The superficial muscle of the thenar eminence at the base of the thumb.
abductor pollicis brevis.function: Moves the thumb away from the palm.
abductor pollicis brevis.clinical: Wastes in carpal tunnel syndrome because it is supplied by the median nerve.

flexor pollicis brevis.summary: A thenar muscle with a superficial and a deep head.
flexor pollicis brevis.function: Flexes the thumb at its base.

opponens pollicis.summary: A deep thenar muscle inserting along the first metacarpal.
opponens pollicis.function: Rotates the thumb to touch the fingertips (opposition), the key to a precision grip.

adductor pollicis.summary: A fan-shaped muscle in the web of the thumb with oblique and transverse heads.
adductor pollicis.function: Adducts the thumb and gives the pinch its power.
adductor pollicis.clinical: Weakness produces Froment's sign in ulnar nerve palsy.

abductor digiti minimi of hand.summary: The muscle along the ulnar border of the palm.

flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand.function: Flexes the little finger at its base.

opponens digiti minimi of hand.summary: A deep hypothenar muscle along the fifth metacarpal.
opponens digiti minimi of hand.function: Cups the palm by drawing the fifth metacarpal forward.

set of lumbricals of hand.summary: Four slender muscles arising from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus.
set of lumbricals of hand.function: Flex the knuckles while extending the finger joints, the position for holding a pen.

set of dorsal interossei of hand.summary: Four muscles between the metacarpals on the back of the hand.

set of palmar interossei of hand.summary: Three muscles between the metacarpals on the palm side.

flexor retinaculum of wrist.summary: The strong fibrous band across the front of the wrist forming the roof of the carpal tunnel.
flexor retinaculum of wrist.function: Holds the flexor tendons in place; the median nerve passes beneath it.
flexor retinaculum of wrist.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome is treated by dividing this retinaculum.

superior rectus.summary: An extraocular muscle on top of the eyeball, supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

inferior rectus.summary: An extraocular muscle beneath the eyeball.
inferior rectus.clinical: Can be trapped in fractures of the orbital floor, limiting upward gaze.

medial rectus.summary: The extraocular muscle on the inner side of the eyeball.
medial rectus.function: Turns the eye inward toward the nose; both together converge the eyes for near vision.

lateral rectus.summary: The extraocular muscle on the outer side of the eyeball, supplied by the abducens nerve.
lateral rectus.clinical: Abducens palsy causes double vision on looking to that side.

superior oblique.summary: An extraocular muscle whose tendon passes through a fibrous pulley (trochlea) before reaching the eyeball, supplied by the trochlear nerve.
superior oblique.function: Turns the eye down and out and rotates it inward.

inferior oblique.summary: The only extraocular muscle arising from the front of the orbit.
inferior oblique.function: Turns the eye up and out and rotates it outward.

levator palpebrae superioris.summary: The muscle that raises the upper eyelid.
levator palpebrae superioris.function: Opens the eye; its smooth-muscle part keeps the lid up in the alert state.
levator palpebrae superioris.clinical: Weakness causes drooping of the eyelid (ptosis).

common tendinous ring.summary: The fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit from which the four rectus muscles arise.
common tendinous ring.function: Anchors the rectus muscles; the optic nerve and the nerves to the eye muscles pass through it.

genioglossus.summary: The large fan-shaped muscle forming the bulk of the tongue, from the inside of the chin.
genioglossus.function: Protrudes the tongue and pulls it forward, keeping the airway open in sleep.
genioglossus.clinical: Hypoglossal nerve palsy makes the tongue deviate toward the weak side.

hyoglossus.summary: A thin muscle from the hyoid bone into the side of the tongue.

geniohyoid.summary: A narrow muscle from the chin to the hyoid bone.
geniohyoid.function: Pulls the hyoid forward and up during swallowing.

mylohyoid.summary: The muscular floor of the mouth, stretched between the two sides of the mandible.
mylohyoid.function: Raises the floor of the mouth and the tongue in swallowing.

digastric.summary: A muscle with two bellies joined by a tendon slung from the hyoid bone.
digastric.function: Opens the mouth by lowering the mandible and raises the hyoid in swallowing.

stylohyoid.summary: A slender muscle from the styloid process to the hyoid bone.
stylohyoid.function: Pulls the hyoid up and back.

sternohyoid.summary: A strap muscle in the front of the neck from the sternum to the hyoid.

sternothyroid.summary: A strap muscle from the sternum to the thyroid cartilage.

thyrohyoid.summary: A short muscle from the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid.
thyrohyoid.function: Raises the larynx or depresses the hyoid.

omohyoid.summary: A two-bellied strap muscle running from the scapula across the neck to the hyoid.
omohyoid.function: Depresses the hyoid and tenses the deep cervical fascia.

longus capitis.summary: A deep muscle on the front of the cervical spine reaching the skull base.

longus colli.summary: A deep muscle along the front of the cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae.
longus colli.function: Flexes the neck and steadies the cervical spine.

rectus capitis anterior.summary: A small muscle from the atlas to the skull base.
rectus capitis anterior.function: Flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.

rectus capitis lateralis.summary: A small muscle from the atlas to the jugular process of the occipital bone.

rectus capitis posterior major.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the spine of the axis to the occipital bone.

rectus capitis posterior minor.summary: A small suboccipital muscle from the atlas to the occipital bone.

obliquus capitis superior.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the atlas to the occipital bone.
obliquus capitis superior.function: Extends the head and bends it sideways.

obliquus capitis inferior.summary: A suboccipital muscle from the axis to the atlas.
obliquus capitis inferior.function: Rotates the atlas, turning the head.

splenius capitis.summary: A broad strap muscle from the spine to the skull base, lying under trapezius.
splenius capitis.function: Extends and rotates the head; together, both sides pull the head back.

splenius cervicis.summary: The lower part of the splenius, from the upper thoracic spines to the cervical transverse processes.

semispinalis capitis.summary: A thick muscle of the back of the neck from the upper spine to the occipital bone.
semispinalis capitis.function: Extends the head and neck; a common source of tension headache.

semispinalis cervicis.summary: A deep muscle from the upper thoracic to the cervical vertebrae.
semispinalis cervicis.function: Extends and rotates the cervical spine.

semispinalis thoracis.summary: A deep back muscle spanning the thoracic vertebrae.
semispinalis thoracis.function: Extends and rotates the thoracic spine.

longissimus capitis.summary: The part of the erector spinae reaching the mastoid process.

longissimus cervicis.summary: The part of the erector spinae inserting on the cervical vertebrae.

longissimus thoracis.summary: The largest column of the erector spinae, along the thoracic and lumbar spine.
longissimus thoracis.function: Extends the spine and keeps the trunk upright.

iliocostalis lumborum.summary: The lateral column of the erector spinae in the lumbar region, reaching the lower ribs.
iliocostalis lumborum.function: Extends and bends the lumbar spine.

iliocostalis thoracis.summary: The middle part of the iliocostalis, running between the ribs.
iliocostalis thoracis.function: Extends the thoracic spine and steadies the ribs.

iliocostalis cervicis.summary: The upper part of the iliocostalis, from the upper ribs to the cervical vertebrae.

spinalis thoracis.summary: The medial column of the erector spinae, closest to the spinous processes.

spinalis.summary: The medial column of the erector spinae, closest to the spinous processes.

interspinalis thoracis.summary: Short muscles between adjacent spinous processes.
interspinalis thoracis.function: Extend the spine and stabilise the vertebrae.

set of interspinales cervicis.summary: Short paired muscles between the cervical spinous processes.
set of interspinales cervicis.function: Extend the neck and steady the vertebrae.

set of interspinales lumborum.summary: Short muscles between the lumbar spinous processes.
set of interspinales lumborum.function: Extend and stabilise the lumbar spine.

lateral lumbar intertransversarius.summary: Small muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.
lateral lumbar intertransversarius.function: Bend the spine sideways and stabilise it.

medial lumbar intertransversarius.summary: Small deep muscles between the lumbar transverse processes.

set of anterior cervical intertransversa.summary: Small muscles between the cervical transverse processes.

set of posterior cervical intertransvers.summary: Small muscles between the cervical transverse processes behind the spinal nerves.

cervical rotator.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the cervical spine.

thoracic rotator.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the thoracic spine, from transverse to spinous processes.
thoracic rotator.function: Rotate and stabilise the vertebrae; rich in sensors that report spinal position.

lumbar rotator.summary: Deep rotator muscles of the lumbar spine.
lumbar rotator.function: Rotate and stabilise the lumbar vertebrae.

serratus posterior superior.summary: A thin muscle of the upper back from the spine to the upper ribs.
serratus posterior superior.function: Elevates the upper ribs in inspiration.

serratus posterior inferior.summary: A thin muscle of the lower back from the spine to the lower ribs.
serratus posterior inferior.function: Pulls the lower ribs down and out.

set of levatores costarum breves.summary: Short muscles from the transverse processes to the rib below.

set of levatores costarum longi.summary: Longer muscles from the transverse processes skipping one rib.

external anal sphincter.summary: The ring of voluntary muscle around the anal canal.
external anal sphincter.clinical: Injury in childbirth or surgery can cause incontinence.

puborectalis.summary: A U-shaped sling of the levator ani looping behind the anorectal junction.
puborectalis.function: Kinks the rectum forward to maintain continence and relaxes during defecation.

pubococcygeus.summary: The main part of the levator ani, from the pubis to the coccyx.
pubococcygeus.function: Supports the pelvic organs and helps continence.

iliococcygeus.summary: The lateral part of the levator ani, from the tendinous arch to the coccyx.

coccygeus.summary: A muscle behind the levator ani from the ischial spine to the coccyx.
coccygeus.function: Supports the pelvic floor and flexes the coccyx.

tendinous arch of levator ani.summary: The thickened fascia on the inside of the pelvis from which the levator ani arises.

superficial perineal muscle.summary: Muscles of the superficial perineal pouch.
superficial perineal muscle.function: Support the perineum and contribute to erection and ejaculation.

superior pharyngeal constrictor.summary: The uppermost of the three overlapping muscles of the pharyngeal wall.
superior pharyngeal constrictor.function: Squeezes the top of the pharynx to push the food bolus downward.

middle pharyngeal constrictor.summary: The middle constrictor of the pharynx, from the hyoid bone.

inferior pharyngeal constrictor.summary: The lowest and thickest pharyngeal constrictor, from the larynx.
inferior pharyngeal constrictor.function: Completes the swallow and its lower fibres act as the upper oesophageal sphincter.

stylopharyngeus.summary: A long muscle from the styloid process into the pharynx, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
stylopharyngeus.function: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing.

palatopharyngeus.summary: A muscle from the soft palate down into the pharynx.
palatopharyngeus.function: Pulls the pharynx up and narrows the throat in swallowing.

salpingopharyngeus.summary: A slender muscle from the auditory tube into the pharynx.
salpingopharyngeus.function: Raises the pharynx and helps open the auditory tube.

levator veli palatini.summary: A muscle from the skull base into the soft palate.
levator veli palatini.function: Lifts the soft palate to close the nose off during swallowing and speech.

tensor veli palatini.summary: A muscle whose tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus into the soft palate.
tensor veli palatini.function: Tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube (the 'pop' when swallowing).

uvular muscle.summary: The small muscle inside the uvula.

pharyngeal raphe.summary: The fibrous seam down the midline of the back of the pharynx.
pharyngeal raphe.function: Joins the constrictor muscles of the two sides.

pterygomandibular raphe.summary: A fibrous band between the buccinator and the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
pterygomandibular raphe.function: Shared attachment for the cheek and pharynx muscles.

cricothyroid.summary: A muscle on the outside of the larynx between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, the only laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
cricothyroid.function: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to stretch the vocal ligaments and raise the pitch of the voice.

posterior crico-arytenoid.summary: A muscle on the back of the cricoid cartilage.
posterior crico-arytenoid.function: The only muscle that opens the vocal folds; essential for breathing.
posterior crico-arytenoid.clinical: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyses it and obstructs the airway.

lateral crico-arytenoid.summary: A small laryngeal muscle from the cricoid arch to the arytenoid.
lateral crico-arytenoid.function: Closes the vocal folds for phonation.

transverse arytenoid.summary: An unpaired muscle joining the two arytenoid cartilages.
transverse arytenoid.function: Closes the back of the glottis.

oblique arytenoid.summary: A muscle crossing from one arytenoid to the other.
oblique arytenoid.function: Closes the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

thyro-arytenoid.summary: A muscle inside the vocal fold from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid.
thyro-arytenoid.function: Relaxes and shortens the vocal ligament, lowering the pitch.

vocalis.summary: The inner part of the thyroarytenoid lying beside the vocal ligament.
vocalis.function: Fine-tunes the tension of the vocal fold.

aryepiglotticus.summary: A muscle in the aryepiglottic fold.
aryepiglotticus.function: Helps close the inlet of the larynx during swallowing.

intermediate tendon.summary: A tendon joining two muscle bellies.
intermediate tendon.function: Transmits force between the two bellies of a muscle such as the digastric or omohyoid.

trachea.summary: The windpipe: a tube about 11 cm long, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings, from the larynx to the bronchi.
trachea.function: Conducts air to and from the lungs while its lining traps and sweeps out dust.
trachea.clinical: A tracheostomy opens the trachea below the larynx to secure the airway.

left main bronchus.summary: The airway to the left lung, longer and more horizontal than the right.
left main bronchus.function: Conducts air to the left lung and divides into the upper and lower lobe bronchi.

right main bronchus proper.summary: The airway to the right lung, shorter, wider and more vertical than the left.
right main bronchus proper.function: Conducts air to the right lung.
right main bronchus proper.clinical: Inhaled objects usually lodge in the right main bronchus because of its straighter course.

thyroid cartilage.summary: The largest laryngeal cartilage, whose front angle forms the Adam's apple.
thyroid cartilage.function: Shields the larynx and anchors the vocal ligaments.

cricoid cartilage.summary: A complete ring of cartilage below the thyroid cartilage, the only full ring in the airway.
cricoid cartilage.function: Supports the larynx and the arytenoid cartilages that move the vocal folds.
cricoid cartilage.clinical: Pressure on the cricoid can compress the oesophagus during emergency intubation.

arytenoid cartilage.summary: A pyramid-shaped cartilage on top of the cricoid.
arytenoid cartilage.function: Its rotation opens and closes the vocal folds.

corniculate cartilage.summary: A small nodule of cartilage on the apex of each arytenoid.

cuneiform cartilage.summary: A small rod of cartilage in the aryepiglottic fold.

epiglottis.summary: A leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage behind the tongue.
epiglottis.function: Folds down over the larynx during swallowing to keep food out of the airway.
epiglottis.clinical: Acute epiglottitis can obstruct the airway.

vocal ligament.summary: The elastic core of the vocal fold, from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid.
vocal ligament.function: Vibrates in the airstream to produce the voice.

conus elasticus.summary: The elastic membrane of the lower larynx, whose upper edge is the vocal ligament.
conus elasticus.clinical: Emergency cricothyroidotomy passes through the cricothyroid membrane in front of it.

thyrohyoid membrane.summary: A sheet of fibrous tissue joining the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone.
thyrohyoid membrane.function: Suspends the larynx from the hyoid; the internal laryngeal nerve pierces it.

median cricothyroid ligament.summary: The midline part of the cricothyroid membrane.
median cricothyroid ligament.clinical: The site for emergency cricothyroidotomy when the airway is blocked above.

hyo-epiglottic ligament.summary: An elastic band from the hyoid bone to the epiglottis.
hyo-epiglottic ligament.function: Anchors the front of the epiglottis.

thyro-epiglottic ligament.summary: A ligament fixing the stalk of the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage.

septal nasal cartilage.summary: The cartilage of the nasal septum in front of the vomer and ethmoid.
septal nasal cartilage.function: Divides the nostrils and supports the nose.
septal nasal cartilage.clinical: Deviation causes blockage; septoplasty straightens it.

lateral nasal cartilage.summary: A triangular cartilage forming the side of the nose below the nasal bone.

major alar cartilage.summary: A U-shaped cartilage surrounding the nostril and forming the nasal tip.

esophagus.summary: The oesophagus: a 25 cm muscular tube carrying food from the pharynx through the chest to the stomach.
esophagus.function: Peristaltic waves push swallowed food downward; the lower sphincter stops stomach acid returning.
esophagus.clinical: Reflux, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal cancer; swallowing difficulty (dysphagia) needs investigation.

stomach.summary: The J-shaped muscular sac in the upper left abdomen where food is stored and churned with acid and pepsin.
stomach.function: Begins protein digestion, kills microbes with acid and releases chyme into the duodenum in measured amounts.
stomach.clinical: Peptic ulcers (often from Helicobacter pylori), gastritis and gastric cancer.

duodenum.summary: The first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, curving around the head of the pancreas.
duodenum.function: Receives chyme, bile and pancreatic juice and neutralises stomach acid.
duodenum.clinical: The commonest site of peptic ulcers.

appendix.summary: A blind-ended worm-like tube hanging from the caecum.
appendix.function: Contains lymphoid tissue; its role in digestion is negligible.
appendix.clinical: Appendicitis is the commonest cause of emergency abdominal surgery.

ascending colon.summary: The part of the large intestine rising up the right side of the abdomen from the caecum.
ascending colon.function: Absorbs water and salts from the intestinal contents.

transverse colon.summary: The longest, most mobile part of the colon, hanging across the abdomen below the stomach.
transverse colon.function: Continues water absorption and moves stool toward the descending colon.

descending colon.summary: The part of the colon running down the left side of the abdomen.
descending colon.function: Stores faeces before they pass into the sigmoid colon.
descending colon.clinical: Diverticular disease and cancer are commoner on the left side of the colon.

rectum.summary: The final 12 cm of the large intestine, in the pelvis in front of the sacrum.
rectum.function: Stores faeces and signals the need to defecate.
rectum.clinical: Rectal bleeding and change of bowel habit are warning signs of colorectal cancer.

taenia libera.summary: One of the three longitudinal bands of muscle on the colon, the free band not attached to mesentery.
taenia libera.function: Shortens the colon into its pouches (haustra).

taenia mesocolica.summary: The longitudinal muscle band of the colon along the attachment of the mesocolon.

taenia omentalis.summary: The longitudinal muscle band of the colon along the attachment of the greater omentum.

ileocecal junction.summary: Where the ileum enters the caecum, guarded by the ileocaecal valve.
ileocecal junction.function: Regulates flow into the large intestine and prevents backflow.

mesentery of small intestine.summary: The fan-shaped fold of peritoneum that suspends the jejunum and ileum from the back wall of the abdomen.
mesentery of small intestine.function: Carries the vessels, nerves and lymphatics of the small intestine.
mesentery of small intestine.clinical: Twisting of the mesentery (volvulus) cuts off the blood supply to the bowel.

mesoappendix.summary: The small fold of peritoneum carrying the appendicular artery to the appendix.

transverse mesocolon.summary: The fold of peritoneum suspending the transverse colon from the back wall of the abdomen.

tongue.summary: A muscular organ in the floor of the mouth covered with taste buds.
tongue.function: Moves food, shapes speech and senses taste; the genioglossus keeps it from falling back in sleep.
tongue.clinical: Oral cancers commonly arise on the side of the tongue.

gingiva of upper jaw.summary: The gums surrounding the upper teeth.
gingiva of upper jaw.function: Seal the teeth against the jaw and resist chewing forces.
gingiva of upper jaw.clinical: Gingivitis and periodontitis are among the commonest diseases worldwide.

gingiva of lower jaw.summary: The gums surrounding the lower teeth.
gingiva of lower jaw.function: Seal the teeth against the jaw and resist chewing forces.

lip.summary: The fleshy folds surrounding the mouth.
lip.function: Seal the mouth, hold food and shape speech and expression.

submandibular gland.summary: A walnut-sized salivary gland beneath the jaw.
submandibular gland.function: Produces most of the saliva at rest, opening beneath the tongue.
submandibular gland.clinical: The commonest site of salivary stones.

sublingual gland.summary: The smallest of the major salivary glands, under the tongue.
sublingual gland.function: Secretes thick, mucous saliva through many small ducts.

gallbladder.summary: A pear-shaped sac beneath the liver storing about 50 ml of bile.
gallbladder.function: Concentrates bile and squirts it into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.
gallbladder.clinical: Gallstones can cause colic, cholecystitis and jaundice; removal (cholecystectomy) is one of the commonest operations.

cystic duct.summary: The short duct joining the gallbladder to the common bile duct.

common hepatic duct.summary: The duct formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts, carrying bile out of the liver.

right hepatic duct.summary: The duct draining bile from the right half of the liver.

left hepatic duct.summary: The duct draining bile from the left half of the liver.

caudate lobe of liver.summary: A small lobe on the back of the liver between the vena cava and the ligamentum venosum (segment I).
caudate lobe of liver.function: Drains directly into the inferior vena cava, so it is spared in some liver diseases.

duct of caudate lobe of liver.summary: A bile duct draining the caudate lobe.

pancreas.summary: A soft, elongated gland lying across the back of the abdomen behind the stomach.
pancreas.function: Its exocrine tissue makes enzymes for digesting fat, protein and starch; its islets secrete insulin and glucagon.
pancreas.clinical: Pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer and type 1 diabetes.

parenchyma of pancreas.summary: The glandular tissue of the pancreas.
parenchyma of pancreas.function: Produces digestive enzymes and the hormones of the islets.

pancreatic duct.summary: The main duct running the length of the pancreas to the duodenum.
pancreatic duct.function: Carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum, usually joining the bile duct at the ampulla.
pancreatic duct.clinical: Blockage by a stone or tumour causes pancreatitis or jaundice.

pancreatic duct tree.summary: The branching system of ducts collecting enzyme-rich juice from the pancreatic lobules.

spleen.summary: A soft, fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen under the ribs.
spleen.function: Filters the blood, removes worn-out red cells and mounts immune responses to blood-borne infection.
spleen.clinical: Ruptures in abdominal trauma; people without a spleen need vaccination against encapsulated bacteria.

kidney.summary: A bean-shaped organ on the back wall of the abdomen; the left lies slightly higher than the right.
kidney.function: Filters the blood to form urine, balances water and salts, regulates blood pressure and makes erythropoietin.
kidney.clinical: Kidney stones, infections and chronic kidney disease; a single healthy kidney is enough for normal life.

ureter.summary: A 25 cm muscular tube from the renal pelvis to the bladder.
ureter.function: Peristalsis carries urine to the bladder; the ureter tunnels obliquely into the bladder wall to prevent backflow.
ureter.clinical: Stones lodging in the ureter cause severe colicky pain.

urinary bladder.summary: A hollow muscular organ in the pelvis that stores urine.
urinary bladder.function: Expands to hold about 400 to 600 ml, then contracts (the detrusor) to empty through the urethra.
urinary bladder.clinical: Urinary tract infections, overactive bladder and bladder cancer.

urethra.summary: The tube carrying urine from the bladder out of the body: about 4 cm long in the female, opening just in front of the vagina; about 20 cm in the male, where it also carries semen and runs through the prostate and penis.
urethra.clinical: The short female urethra is one reason urinary infections are commoner in women. Urethral strictures and injuries; the prostatic part is compressed in prostatic enlargement.

prostate.summary: A walnut-sized gland surrounding the first part of the urethra below the bladder.
prostate.function: Secretes fluid that makes up about a third of semen.
prostate.clinical: Benign enlargement slows the urinary stream in older men; prostate cancer is among the commonest male cancers. The prostate is kept in vaginoplasty, so prostate care still applies to trans women.

testis.summary: The male gonad, suspended in the scrotum where it is cooler than the body core.
testis.clinical: Testicular torsion is an emergency; testicular cancer mostly affects young men.

epididymis.summary: A tightly coiled tube on the back of the testis.
epididymis.function: Stores sperm while they mature and gain the ability to swim.

deferent duct.summary: The vas deferens: a thick-walled tube carrying sperm from the epididymis through the inguinal canal to the ejaculatory duct.

seminal vesicle.summary: A coiled gland behind the bladder.
seminal vesicle.function: Produces most of the volume of semen, rich in fructose.

corpus cavernosum of penis.summary: One of the two erectile cylinders along the top of the penis.
corpus cavernosum of penis.function: Fills with blood to produce an erection.

corpus spongiosum of penis.summary: The erectile body surrounding the urethra, ending in the glans.
corpus spongiosum of penis.function: Keeps the urethra open during erection.

glans penis.summary: The expanded sensitive tip of the penis, formed by the corpus spongiosum.

adrenal gland.summary: A small triangular gland sitting on top of the kidney.
adrenal gland.function: The cortex makes cortisol, aldosterone and androgens; the medulla releases adrenaline in stress.
adrenal gland.clinical: Addison's disease (failure) and Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol).

pituitary gland.summary: A pea-sized gland hanging from the hypothalamus in a bony hollow of the sphenoid.
pituitary gland.function: The 'master gland': controls growth, thyroid, adrenal and reproductive function and water balance.
pituitary gland.clinical: Pituitary tumours can press on the optic chiasm, narrowing the visual fields.

left lobe of thymus.summary: One of the two lobes of the thymus behind the sternum.
left lobe of thymus.function: Trains T lymphocytes in childhood; the gland shrinks after puberty.

right lobe of thymus.summary: One of the two lobes of the thymus behind the sternum.
right lobe of thymus.function: Trains T lymphocytes in childhood; the gland shrinks after puberty.

cerebellum.summary: The 'little brain' behind the brainstem, with two hemispheres and a central vermis.
cerebellum.function: Coordinates balance, posture and the timing and smoothness of movement; also contributes to learning and language.
cerebellum.clinical: Damage causes unsteady gait, tremor and slurred speech; alcohol acts on it acutely.

pons.summary: The bulging middle part of the brainstem between the midbrain and medulla.
pons.function: Relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and houses nuclei controlling breathing, sleep and facial sensation and movement.

medulla oblongata.summary: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.
medulla oblongata.function: Controls heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, swallowing and vomiting; the motor fibres cross here.
medulla oblongata.clinical: Compression by raised pressure (coning) is fatal.

midbrain.summary: The upper part of the brainstem, joining the pons to the forebrain.
midbrain.function: Carries the visual and auditory reflex centres (colliculi), the substantia nigra of movement and the nuclei of the eye-movement nerves.
midbrain.clinical: Loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.

peduncle of midbrain.summary: The cerebral peduncle: the thick bundles of fibres on the front of the midbrain.
peduncle of midbrain.function: Carries motor fibres from the cerebral cortex to the brainstem and spinal cord.

thalamus.summary: A pair of egg-shaped masses of grey matter deep in the brain on either side of the third ventricle.
thalamus.function: The gateway to the cortex: almost every sensory pathway is relayed here, and it regulates consciousness and attention.
thalamus.clinical: Thalamic stroke can produce loss of sensation or chronic pain on the opposite side.

hypothalamus.summary: A small region beneath the thalamus forming the floor of the third ventricle.
hypothalamus.function: Controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, hormones (via the pituitary) and the autonomic nervous system.

caudate nucleus.summary: A C-shaped nucleus of the basal ganglia curving around the lateral ventricle.
caudate nucleus.function: Part of the circuits that plan and select movements and habits.

putamen.summary: The outer part of the lentiform nucleus of the basal ganglia.
putamen.function: Regulates movement together with the caudate nucleus.
putamen.clinical: A common site of hypertensive brain haemorrhage.

globus pallidus.summary: The inner, paler part of the lentiform nucleus.
globus pallidus.function: The main output station of the basal ganglia, releasing intended movements.
globus pallidus.clinical: A target for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.

amygdala.summary: An almond-shaped nucleus in the front of the temporal lobe.
amygdala.function: Processes fear, emotion and emotional memory.

hippocampus.summary: A curled ridge of cortex in the medial temporal lobe.
hippocampus.function: Forms new memories and helps with spatial navigation.
hippocampus.clinical: One of the first regions damaged in Alzheimer's disease; a common source of epilepsy.

corpus callosum.summary: The largest bundle of fibres in the brain, arching over the ventricles.
corpus callosum.function: Connects the two cerebral hemispheres so they share information.
corpus callosum.clinical: Surgical division was once used to control severe epilepsy.

fornix of forebrain.summary: A C-shaped bundle of fibres arching from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
fornix of forebrain.function: The main output pathway of the hippocampus for memory.

commissure of fornix of forebrain.summary: The fibres crossing between the two fornices beneath the corpus callosum.

internal capsule.summary: A dense band of white matter between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus.
internal capsule.function: Carries nearly all fibres between the cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord.
internal capsule.clinical: A small stroke here can paralyse the whole opposite side of the body.

insula.summary: A region of cortex hidden deep in the lateral fissure.
insula.function: Processes taste, visceral sensation, pain and emotional awareness of the body.

precentral gyrus.summary: The gyrus in front of the central sulcus: the primary motor cortex.
precentral gyrus.function: Sends the commands for voluntary movement of the opposite side of the body, mapped as the motor homunculus.
precentral gyrus.clinical: Damage causes weakness (upper motor neuron signs) on the opposite side.

postcentral gyrus.summary: The gyrus behind the central sulcus: the primary somatosensory cortex.
postcentral gyrus.function: Receives touch, pressure, pain and position sense from the opposite side of the body.

superior frontal gyrus.summary: The uppermost of the three frontal gyri.
superior frontal gyrus.function: Involved in planning, self-awareness and the supplementary motor area.

middle frontal gyrus.summary: The middle gyrus of the lateral frontal lobe.
middle frontal gyrus.function: Working memory, attention and eye movement control (frontal eye field).

inferior frontal gyrus.summary: The lowest frontal gyrus, containing Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere.

superior temporal gyrus.summary: The uppermost temporal gyrus, containing the auditory cortex and Wernicke's area.
superior temporal gyrus.function: Hearing and the understanding of language.
superior temporal gyrus.clinical: Damage to Wernicke's area causes fluent but meaningless speech.

middle temporal gyrus.summary: The middle gyrus of the lateral temporal lobe.
middle temporal gyrus.function: Contributes to word meaning, face recognition and visual motion perception.

fusiform gyrus.summary: A gyrus on the underside of the temporal lobe.

parahippocampal gyrus.summary: The gyrus on the medial temporal lobe surrounding the hippocampus.
parahippocampal gyrus.function: Memory encoding and the recognition of scenes.

cingulate gyrus.summary: The gyrus arching above the corpus callosum on the inner face of the hemisphere.
cingulate gyrus.function: Part of the limbic system: emotion, pain, error detection and attention.

angular gyrus.summary: A gyrus at the back of the parietal lobe where the temporal and occipital lobes meet.
angular gyrus.function: Reading, arithmetic and linking words to meaning.

supramarginal gyrus.summary: A gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule curling over the end of the lateral fissure.
supramarginal gyrus.function: Language, touch perception and body awareness.

superior parietal lobule.summary: The upper part of the parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus.
superior parietal lobule.function: Spatial awareness and guiding movements with the eyes and hands.

occipital lobe.summary: The lobe at the back of the brain.
occipital lobe.function: The visual cortex: interprets everything the eyes see.
occipital lobe.clinical: Damage causes loss of the opposite visual field.

orbital gyrus.summary: The gyri on the underside of the frontal lobe above the orbit.

white matter of cerebral hemisphere.summary: The mass of myelinated fibres beneath the cortex.
white matter of cerebral hemisphere.function: Connects cortical areas with each other and with the rest of the nervous system.
white matter of cerebral hemisphere.clinical: Multiple sclerosis attacks white matter myelin.

septum of telencephalon.summary: The septal region at the front of the brain below the corpus callosum.
septum of telencephalon.function: Part of the reward and emotion circuits of the limbic system.

septum pellucidum.summary: A thin double membrane separating the two lateral ventricles.

lateral ventricle.summary: The large C-shaped fluid-filled cavity inside each cerebral hemisphere.
lateral ventricle.clinical: Enlarges in hydrocephalus and with brain atrophy.

third ventricle.summary: The narrow midline cavity between the two thalami.
third ventricle.function: Passes cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles to the aqueduct.

fourth ventricle.summary: The diamond-shaped cavity between the brainstem and cerebellum.
fourth ventricle.function: Releases cerebrospinal fluid into the subarachnoid space.

cerebral aqueduct.summary: The narrow channel through the midbrain joining the third and fourth ventricles.

interventricular foramen.summary: The opening between each lateral ventricle and the third ventricle.

choroid plexus of cerebral hemisphere.summary: The frilly vascular tissue in the ventricles.
choroid plexus of cerebral hemisphere.function: Secretes about half a litre of cerebrospinal fluid a day.

central canal of spinal cord.summary: The tiny channel running down the centre of the spinal cord, continuous with the fourth ventricle.

anterior commissure.summary: A small bundle of fibres crossing the midline in front of the fornix.
anterior commissure.function: Connects the temporal lobes and olfactory regions of the two sides.

posterior commissure.summary: A bundle of fibres crossing at the back of the third ventricle.
posterior commissure.function: Carries fibres for the pupillary light reflex.

habenula.summary: A small nucleus at the back of the thalamus beside the pineal.
habenula.function: Links the limbic system to the brainstem; involved in reward and aversion.

stria medullaris of thalamus.summary: A fibre bundle running along the top of the thalamus to the habenula.

stria terminalis.summary: A slender fibre bundle from the amygdala following the curve of the caudate nucleus.
stria terminalis.function: Carries output from the amygdala to the hypothalamus.

lamina terminalis.summary: The thin front wall of the third ventricle.
lamina terminalis.function: Contains sensors for blood osmolarity that drive thirst.

tuber cinereum.summary: The grey hump of the hypothalamus from which the pituitary stalk arises.
tuber cinereum.function: Releases the hormones that control the anterior pituitary.

mammillary body.summary: One of two small rounded bodies on the underside of the hypothalamus.
mammillary body.function: A relay in the memory circuit from the hippocampus.
mammillary body.clinical: Damaged by thiamine deficiency in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

pineal body.summary: A small pine-cone shaped gland at the back of the third ventricle.
pineal body.function: Secretes melatonin, setting the sleep-wake rhythm.

superior colliculus.summary: The upper of the two bumps on the back of the midbrain.
superior colliculus.function: Directs the eyes and head toward visual stimuli.

inferior colliculus.summary: The lower bump on the back of the midbrain.
inferior colliculus.function: Relays hearing and drives reflex turning toward sounds.

brachium of superior colliculus.summary: The fibre band carrying visual fibres to the superior colliculus.

brachium of inferior colliculus.summary: The fibre band carrying auditory fibres from the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.

lateral geniculate body.summary: The visual relay nucleus of the thalamus.
lateral geniculate body.function: Passes signals from the optic tract to the visual cortex.

medial geniculate body.summary: The auditory relay nucleus of the thalamus.
medial geniculate body.function: Passes sound signals to the auditory cortex.

interpeduncular fossa.summary: The hollow between the cerebral peduncles on the underside of the midbrain, where the oculomotor nerves emerge.

tentorium cerebelli.summary: The tent-shaped fold of dura mater separating the cerebellum from the occipital lobes.
tentorium cerebelli.clinical: A swelling brain can herniate through its opening, compressing the brainstem.

optic nerve.summary: The second cranial nerve, carrying about a million fibres from the retina to the optic chiasm.
optic nerve.function: Transmits vision from the eye to the brain.
optic nerve.clinical: Optic neuritis, often the first sign of multiple sclerosis, and glaucoma damage its fibres.

optic chiasm.summary: The X-shaped crossing of the optic nerves above the pituitary gland.
optic chiasm.function: Fibres from the nasal halves of each retina cross, so each hemisphere sees the opposite visual field.
optic chiasm.clinical: Compression by a pituitary tumour causes loss of both outer visual fields.

optic tract.summary: The visual pathway from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate body.
optic tract.function: Carries the opposite visual field to the thalamus.

superior branch of oculomotor nerve.summary: The upper division of the third cranial nerve.
superior branch of oculomotor nerve.function: Supplies the superior rectus and the levator of the upper eyelid.

inferior branch of oculomotor nerve.summary: The lower division of the third cranial nerve.
inferior branch of oculomotor nerve.function: Supplies the medial and inferior rectus, the inferior oblique and the parasympathetic fibres to the pupil.

trochlear nerve.summary: The fourth cranial nerve, the thinnest and the only one emerging from the back of the brainstem.
trochlear nerve.function: Supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye.
trochlear nerve.clinical: Palsy causes vertical double vision, worst when looking down stairs.

ophthalmic nerve.summary: The first division of the trigeminal nerve, entering the orbit.
ophthalmic nerve.function: Carries sensation from the eye, forehead, upper eyelid and nose.
ophthalmic nerve.clinical: Shingles in this nerve can involve the eye.

frontal nerve.summary: The largest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, running along the roof of the orbit.
frontal nerve.function: Sensation from the forehead and scalp via the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves.

supra-orbital nerve.summary: A branch of the frontal nerve leaving the orbit through the supraorbital notch.
supra-orbital nerve.function: Sensation from the forehead and front of the scalp.

supratrochlear nerve.summary: A branch of the frontal nerve passing above the trochlea.
supratrochlear nerve.function: Sensation from the middle of the forehead and upper eyelid.

lacrimal nerve.summary: The smallest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, along the outer wall of the orbit.
lacrimal nerve.function: Sensation from the lacrimal gland, conjunctiva and outer upper eyelid.

nasociliary nerve.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic nerve crossing the orbit to the nose.
nasociliary nerve.function: Sensation from the eyeball, the nasal cavity and the skin of the nose.

long ciliary nerve.summary: A branch of the nasociliary nerve passing to the eyeball.
long ciliary nerve.function: Sensation from the cornea and sympathetic fibres to the pupil.

short ciliary nerve.summary: Small nerves from the ciliary ganglion to the eyeball.
short ciliary nerve.function: Carry parasympathetic fibres that constrict the pupil and focus the lens.

ciliary ganglion.summary: A tiny parasympathetic ganglion in the back of the orbit.
ciliary ganglion.function: Relays the nerves that constrict the pupil and thicken the lens for near vision.

anterior ethmoidal nerve.summary: A branch of the nasociliary nerve entering the nasal cavity.
anterior ethmoidal nerve.function: Sensation from the front of the nasal cavity and the tip of the nose.

posterior ethmoidal nerve.summary: A small branch of the nasociliary nerve to the ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses.

infratrochlear nerve.summary: The terminal branch of the nasociliary nerve below the trochlea.
infratrochlear nerve.function: Sensation from the inner corner of the eye and the side of the nose.

communicating branch of nasociliary nerv.summary: The sensory root of the ciliary ganglion, carrying sensation from the eyeball.

cornea.summary: The transparent dome at the front of the eye.
cornea.function: Provides about two thirds of the eye's focusing power; it has no blood vessels and is densely supplied with pain fibres.
cornea.clinical: Scratches heal quickly but ulcers can scar; laser surgery reshapes it to correct vision.

sclera.summary: The tough white outer coat of the eyeball.
sclera.function: Protects the eye, keeps its shape and anchors the extraocular muscles.

choroid.summary: The vascular layer between the sclera and retina.
choroid.function: Nourishes the outer retina and absorbs stray light with its pigment.

iris.summary: The coloured ring of muscle in front of the lens.
iris.function: Adjusts the pupil to control how much light enters the eye.

lens.summary: The transparent, elastic disc behind the iris.
lens.function: Changes shape to focus on near or distant objects.
lens.clinical: Clouding of the lens (cataract) is the commonest cause of treatable blindness.
